title: Exploring Turn-taking Cues in Multi-party Human-robot Discussions about Objects

fields.value: Technical system description combined with a field-trial analysis of 373 museum interactions, including systematic manipulation of the robot's turn-taking cues and attention.

quotes.text: In this paper, we present a dialog system that was exhibited at the Swedish National Museum of Science and Technology.

fields.value: Gazing away during a turn-taking cue significantly reduced the likelihood of user speech (main effect of gaze, p<0.001). Without cues, users continued speaking 33.8% of the time, versus 14.8% with the right combined cues. Furhat's attention target also strongly influenced which user responded (p<0.001).

quotes.text: A chi-square test shows that there is a significant main effect on the use of gaze (p<0.001), where gazing away has an inhibiting effect on the likelihood that the user will continue speaking.
Whereas no cue gives a fairly high probability of the user continuing speaking (33.8%), this can be reduced to 14.8% with the right cues.
In this study we will also investigate the effect of the system’s target of attention on who will respond.
The speaker’s gaze can therefore be used by the listener as a cue to the speaker’s current focus of attention, so-called joint attention [19].

fields.value: The paper does not explicitly define robotic gaze or attention. It operationalises attention as Furhat's target (idle, item, user, or all), maintained by an Attention Flow that moves its gaze and neck.

fields.value: Gaze and attention serve turn-taking: the robot signals it is claiming the floor with gaze-away plus a cue (filled pause, breath, or smile), and gaze selects the next speaker (addressee selection). The robot also acts as a passive side participant through backchannels.

quotes.text: The most obvious signal is to use gaze to select the next speaker [11].
Thus, mutual gaze between the speaker and addressee should increase the likelihood of turn-transition.

fields.value: Furhat's attention target strongly influenced which user responded after its questions (p<0.001). When the targeted user was looking back at Furhat, that user was more likely to take the turn (p<0.05).

quotes.text: As can be seen, Furhat’s attention has a strong influence on who will respond (p<0.001).
As can be seen, if the targeted user is looking back at Furhat, that user is more likely to take the turn.

fields.value: Built in IrisTK with two parallel controllers: a Dialog Flow for turn-taking and an Attention Flow that maps 3D target positions to neck and gaze movements. A Situation model fuses Kinect head tracking, close-talking microphones with two parallel cloud ASR recognizers, and touch-table events; a randomized belief model drives responses.

quotes.text: In the Listening state, the Dialog Flow instructs the two speech recognizers to start listening for speech using a certain silence timeout threshold.

fields.value: The paper argues that 2D animated agents suffer from the Mona Lisa effect because agent and user do not share physical space. Citing prior work, it states Furhat's back-projection on a 3D mask improves turn-yielding accuracy.

quotes.text: This is because the agent and user don’t share the same physical space.

Thus, in a multi-party setting, this means that the agent cannot establish exclusive mutual gaze with one of the users, and in situated interaction the object that is the target of the gaze cannot be inferred.

fields.value: The paper presents a multi-party card-sorting dialog system built on the Furhat robot head, which was exhibited in a museum and used by 373 interactions. Field data showed that gaze-away plus a filled pause, smile, or breath reduced users' likelihood of continuing to speak, and that Furhat's attention target strongly influenced which user responded.

RQ2a; RQ2b; RQ3a; RQ3b; RQ4a; RQ4b; RQ5a; RQ5b — The paper examines gaze and attention roles in turn-taking and addressee selection, measures their effects on users' turn-taking, describes how gaze and attention are controlled, and uses the Furhat robot head.
